title: Liveness, Readiness & Startup Probes
intro: Kubernetes doesn't know if your app is actually healthy unless you tell it how to check. A misconfigured probe is one of the most common causes of mysterious restarts and traffic drops in production.

steps.prompt: Check whether the 'web' pod has any probes configured that might be causing trouble.
steps.fake_output:
Name: web
Status: Running
Liveness: http-get http://:8080/healthz delay=0s timeout=1s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
Readiness: http-get http://:8080/ready delay=5s timeout=1s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
Events:
  Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.0.5:8080/healthz": dial tcp connect: connection refused
steps.explanation: describe shows the exact probe config plus a live Events entry showing it's currently failing — that combination is usually enough to diagnose a probe issue without touching anything else.
steps.why: 'kubectl get pod web -o yaml' has the same probe spec but no live Events — describe is strictly better here since the failure is happening right now.

steps.prompt: The liveness probe hits /healthz with no startup delay. See the pod's actual startup log to check if the app is even listening yet.
steps.explanation: The app doesn't start listening until 8 seconds in, but the liveness probe has delay=0s — it starts checking immediately and fails for the first 8 seconds.
steps.why: This is the classic probe-timing bug: logs tell you WHEN the app actually became ready; comparing that against the probe's delay/period/failure-threshold tells you whether the probe config even makes sense for this app's real startup time.

steps.prompt: The liveness probe only allows 3 failures 10s apart (30s total) before killing the container — but startup sometimes takes longer than that under load. Edit the deployment to fix the probe timing.
steps.fake_output: (opens the deployment spec in your default editor — you'd raise livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds, save, and exit)
steps.explanation: There's no dedicated 'kubectl set probe' command — probe fields are edited directly in the pod template spec, same as any other field.
steps.why: You could also 'kubectl apply -f' an updated manifest — edit is faster for a single one-off field change like this, but apply -f is what you'd actually use in a real GitOps workflow so the change is captured in version control too.

steps.prompt: After the fix rolls out, confirm the pod is passing its readiness check and receiving traffic.
steps.fake_output:
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web    1/1     Running   0          45s
steps.explanation: READY 1/1 specifically means the readiness probe is passing — a pod can show STATUS Running with READY 0/1 if it's up but not yet considered ready to receive traffic.
steps.why: This distinction (Running vs Ready) is exactly what trips people up in real incidents: a pod can be 'Running' the whole time while still being pulled out of a Service's endpoints because readiness keeps failing.
